analysis.one_liner: Set consumer standards for Medicare HMOs and Medigap insurers, including emergency care access and premium rating limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees for 19 months until Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written consumer protections into Medicare's private-plan side. Medicare HMOs would have had to cover prudent-layperson emergency care, let women see an OB/GYN without a referral, answer coverage requests within 24 hours, disclose physician bonus arrangements, and face fines and enrollment suspensions for violating the rules. Medigap insurers would have had to charge the same price to everyone in a community, pay out at least 85 cents of every premium dollar in claims, and offer an annual open enrollment window when they could not reject or price against sick applicants.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in HMOs or thinking of enrolling would gain enforceable rights: a 24-hour deadline on coverage decisions, access to emergency rooms and OB/GYNs without gatekeeper hurdles, disclosure of physician incentive plans and provider credentials, a process for appealing denials, and coverage of dialysis and specialist care when traveling. People buying Medigap supplement policies would gain community rating (no charging older or sicker individuals vastly more within an area), a requirement that insurers pay out at least 85% of premiums in claims (up from 75%), and an annual open enrollment period when no one could be denied or priced up for health status. Agents' commission structures would be limited so enrollment pitches were no longer dominated by signing bonuses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors in Medicare HMOs and Medigap plans

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare HMOs to cover emergency services under a 'prudent layperson' standard, without the plan deciding after the fact whether it was a true emergency, and to arrange dialysis and coverage for enrollees temporarily outside the plan's service area [S3].

Bars Medicare HMOs from requiring a referral to see an OB/GYN, requires access to designated centers of excellence for complex and chronic conditions, and requires HMOs to respond to a member's coverage request within 24 hours [S3].

Stops HMO utilization reviewers from being paid based on how many claims they deny, requires denials to be made only by clinically qualified staff, and creates a timely appeal process for denials of coverage [S3].

Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services real enforcement tools against misbehaving Medicare HMOs: civil money penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, up to $10,000 per week for ongoing deficiencies, and suspension of new enrollment until problems are fixed [S3].

Requires HMOs to disclose physician incentive plans and provider credentials to enrollees on request, restricts agent commissions so they are not the dominant part of an agent's pay, bans unrequested door-to-door enrollment visits, and forces repayment of commissions when a new enrollee drops out within 90 days [S3].

Forces Medigap insurers to community-rate premiums within an area, raises the required claims payout (loss ratio) from 75% to 85%, requires prior approval of marketing materials, and creates an annual open enrollment period of at least 30 days in which insurers cannot deny, condition, or discriminate on pricing because of age, health status, or medical condition [S3].

Sets uniform annual open enrollment windows for HMO, Medigap, and Medicare Select plans so beneficiaries can switch plans once a year, and directs the Secretary to answer beneficiary questions through the mail and a toll-free number [S3].

Requires whole-metropolitan-area service areas so HMOs cannot carve out only the healthiest neighborhoods, and requires consultation with network providers before termination decisions, with 45 days' notice and a review process for providers dropped from the network [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare HMOs and Medigap insurers bear the cost: new coverage mandates, a higher minimum claims payout, fines of up to $25,000 per violation plus $10,000 per week for uncorrected problems, commission clawbacks, and the end of door-to-door enrollment tactics. Insurance agents lose commission-driven enrollment. A partial offset for HMOs: the bill creates new federal 'outlier' payments covering up to 50% of costs above a threshold for unusually expensive enrollees, funded within the existing Medicare risk-contract payment pool rather than by beneficiary premiums.

drawbacks.text: The new outlier payments subsidize Medicare HMOs for their most expensive patients — up to 50% of costs above a threshold, funded by reducing the base payment rate to all risk-contract plans — which shifts some of the cost of the patient protections back onto the plans collectively and blunts the bill's savings [S3].

Mandating unlimited inpatient hospital days for HMO members (removing the normal Medicare day limits) and expanded extended-care coverage would substantially raise plan costs, and the bill allows only 'nominal' cost-sharing to offset them, which could push some HMOs to raise premiums, cut optional extras, or leave the Medicare market [S3].

Community rating of Medigap premiums, while protecting older and sicker buyers, would tend to raise prices for younger, healthier beneficiaries who currently pay less; the bill phases the rating bands in over two years rather than eliminating variation immediately [S3].

The 24-hour deadline for responding to coverage requests and the whole-metropolitan-area service-area rule are demanding operational mandates that smaller plans might struggle to meet, and the bill gives the Secretary discretion (with exceptions) rather than phasing them in gradually [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are concrete and enforceable — emergency access, an end to pay-per-denial review, real fines, an 85% minimum claims payout, and guaranteed annual switching windows — and they target practices beneficiaries had no way to fight alone. The main costs fall on the HMOs and Medigap insurers being regulated, not on beneficiaries, though some costs (expanded hospital coverage, outlier subsidies) would flow through Medicare's payment formulas and eventually to taxpayers and all plans in the pool. The generous outlier payment provision is a genuine softening, but the core of the bill is a straightforward consumer-protection package.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce and Ways and Means committees and then to their health subcommittees, and neither ever acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Pete Stark, the senior Democrat on the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, introduced the bill on May 24, 1995, joined by 14 House colleagues including Henry Waxman, Nancy Pelosi, and Charles Rangel [S3].

The bill was referred to the Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day; within two weeks it was sent to the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means and the Health and Environment Subcommittee of Commerce [S5].
In total 21 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

Over the next 19 months the bill never received a subcommittee markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote. Its only further appearance in the record is a second set of introductory remarks by Stark in April 1996, after which no action followed [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare HMOs and Medigap insurers — none of the bill's coverage mandates, penalty provisions, community-rating rules, or 85% payout requirement ever took effect. Beneficiaries got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 21 cosponsors was a Democrat and no Republican signed on; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split shows up in sponsorship, not roll calls.

industries.note: The bill imposes coverage mandates (emergency care, OB/GYN access, 24-hour decisions, expanded hospital days), utilization-review standards, disclosure rules, and fines up to $25,000 per violation plus $10,000 per week, while letting the Secretary suspend their enrollment. The outlier-payment subsidy and a competitive-bidding demonstration partially soften — and partially reshape — how they are paid.

Community rating within an area, a loss-ratio floor raised from 75% to 85%, prior approval of marketing materials, and an annual 30-day guaranteed open enrollment window cut into the industry's pricing freedom and its ability to avoid sick customers, and the bill subjects these insurers to the same intermediate sanctions as HMOs.

Commissions could no longer be the predominant source of an agent's pay, commissions had to be clawed back if a new enrollee left within 90 days, and door-to-door enrollment visits without the individual's request were banned.

industries.industry: Community clinics and essential community providers
industries.note: The bill allows the Secretary to require HMOs to contract with rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers, and similar essential community providers, opening Medicare HMO networks to safety-net providers.
